one_line: A Dogra general and the Ladakhi king he subdued during the 1830s–1840s conquest of Ladakh and the western Tibet frontier.

appearance.age_look: Zorawar appears late 30s, compact and muscular; Tshepal appears mid 30s, medium build and slightly taller, both athletic but not exaggerated.
appearance.face: Zorawar has a square face, medium-brown Dogra complexion, strong jaw, straight nose, trimmed moustache with short beard, and sharp, determined eyes with a stern but controlled default expression; Tshepal has an oval face, fair-to-light-brown Ladakhi complexion with a slight highland flush, softer jawline, straight nose, thin moustache, and observant, thoughtful eyes with a calm, dignified default expression tinged with resignation.
appearance.hair: Zorawar’s hair is black, kept short at the sides and back with a slightly longer top swept back, mostly hidden under a deep-red Dogra-style turban wrapped low and tight with a narrow golden-brown band; Tshepal’s black hair is shoulder-length, straight and neatly tied into a low ponytail at the back with a dark red cord, the top parted slightly off-center, and he wears no crown, only a simple narrow dark-brown woolen headband that sits across his forehead.
appearance.costume: Zorawar wears an early-19th-century Dogra military outfit: over a knee-length, off-white cotton angarkha-style tunic that crosses left over right and ties at the side, he wears a fitted, quilted dark-olive-green cotton coat with subtle vertical stitching, long sleeves, and a slightly flared skirt to mid-thigh; the coat has a high round collar trimmed with muted maroon piping and simple brass toggle fastenings; at his waist is a broad, deep-red woolen kamarband (sash) with a narrow mustard stripe near the edges, tightly wrapped and knotted on his left hip, from which his scabbard hangs; his trousers are narrow, beige churidar-style, gathered neatly at the ankles; he wears sturdy dark-brown leather boots that rise just above the ankle with simple stitching and no modern laces; over his torso he has a plain, functional steel breastplate, slightly curved and strapped with brown leather straps over the shoulders and sides, without ornate embossing; his forearms bear simple brown leather bracers; Tshepal wears an era-accurate Ladakhi noble ensemble: a full-length, dark maroon goncha (robe) of thick wool reaching to his calves, with long, slightly wide sleeves and a wrap-front that closes right over left, the edges bound with a narrow, dark-blue silk facing; under it a glimpse of a pale-cream inner shirt collar is visible; his goncha is cinched with a wide, dark-blue woolen sash wrapped several times around his waist, the loose end tucked neatly; he wears dark-brown felt boots with turned-up rounded toes and a lighter-brown band stitched around the top; over his shoulders rests a muted-ochre woolen shawl/cloak, slightly weathered, draped from his left shoulder across the back and under his right arm, hinting at the cold highland climate; his jewellery is restrained: a single, thin silver earring in his left ear and a simple coral-and-turquoise bead bracelet on his right wrist, signalling Ladakhi noble status without ostentation, and his outfit remains fully modest and draped.
appearance.signature: Zorawar carries a single slightly-curved Dogra tulwar with a steel blade and a simple brass hilt, the sword sheathed in a dark-brown leather scabbard with minimal brass fittings that hangs from his left side on a brown leather belt over his red sash; Tshepal holds a rolled parchment scroll tied with a red cord, symbolising royal decrees and the constrained authority he retained under Dogra control.

ref_desc: Zorawar Singh is a medium-brown, square-faced Dogra officer with a red turban, short black hair, quilted dark-olive coat over an off-white angarkha, beige churidar, leather boots, steel breastplate and a brass-hilted tulwar at his red sash, standing beside Tshepal Namgyal, a fair Ladakhi noble with an oval face, black ponytail and brown headband, wearing a maroon woolen goncha with dark-blue sash, ochre shawl and simple Ladakhi jewellery, holding a tied scroll; their shared palette is deep red, dark olive green, maroon, dark blue and beige.
sheet_prompt: Draw a full-body anime-style model sheet of two historically grounded figures standing side by side against a plain background: Zorawar Singh and Tshepal Namgyal. Zorawar is a compact, muscular Dogra general in his late 30s with a square face, medium-brown complexion, trimmed moustache and short black hair mostly hidden under a deep-red Dogra-style turban with a narrow golden-brown band; he wears a quilted dark-olive-green fitted cotton coat with vertical stitching and maroon piping over a knee-length off-white angarkha-style tunic, beige churidar trousers, dark-brown ankle-high leather boots, a broad deep-red woolen sash at the waist and a plain, curved steel breastplate strapped over his torso, with simple brown leather bracers on his forearms, and a slightly curved steel tulwar with a plain brass hilt in a dark-brown leather scabbard hanging from his left hip. Beside him, Tshepal Namgyal is a slightly taller, medium-built Ladakhi king in his mid 30s with an oval face, fair-to-light-brown highland complexion, thin moustache, thoughtful eyes, and straight black hair tied into a low ponytail, held back with a simple narrow dark-brown woolen headband. He wears a full-length dark maroon woolen goncha robe with long sleeves and a wrap front edged in dark-blue facing, cinched with a wide dark-blue woolen sash, a pale-cream inner collar just visible, dark-brown felt boots with rounded turned-up toes, and a muted-ochre woolen shawl draped from his left shoulder; his only visible jewellery is a thin silver earring and a coral-and-turquoise bracelet. He holds a rolled parchment scroll tied with a red cord. Keep both fully and modestly clothed, use a consistent palette of deep red, dark olive green, maroon, dark blue and beige, and show front-facing, three-quarter and back views plus close-ups of their faces, hair and Zorawar’s tulwar with scabbard and Tshepal’s scroll to clearly define their canonical design.
